sentences.text: Under Alaska law, a pre-incarceration inventory search of an arrestee is justified to prevent the entry of contraband into the jail, protect the arrestee’s property, and protect the jail against claims of lost or damaged property.
However, such a search is unconstitutional if an arrestee is not going to be incarcerated because they can immediately post bail.
In *Zehrung*, the defendant had been booked on a misdemeanor warrant and failure to pay a $25 fine, and could have posted bail almost immediately.
However, officers searched the defendant’s possessions prior to him posting bail, finding evidence that led to him being charged with sexual assault.

The court found the search unconstitutional, concluding that if someone is able to post an established bail when brought to jail, they should be allowed to do so rather than be subject to a pre-incarceration inventory search.
Even if someone does not have enough money on their immediate person, they should be allowed to make a call to get in touch with someone who can post the bail.
In *Gray*, the Court of Appeals relied on *Zehrung* to find unconstitutional a search of an arrestee’s property prior to the arrestee having an opportunity to post a $500 bail.
Police booked the defendant at Mat-Su Pretrial, where employees routinely conducted this type of search almost immediately upon entrance to the facility.
The fact it was routine, however, did not make it permissible.
{client} had an established bail and was not given an opportunity to post it, or to call someone who could post it, before the search.
